user_class: Hackathon entrants preparing submissions under a short deadline
painful_workflow: Turning a working build into a judge-testable submission requires coordinating demo evidence, repository access, README setup steps, Codex session proof, and post-deadline immutability checks across multiple portals and artifacts.
unmet_need: A reliable way to know whether a submission package is complete, runnable, and defensible before the deadline, especially when judges may rely on the demo or sandbox instead of rebuilding locally.
why_now: The submission window closes on July 21, 2026 at 5:00 PM PDT, changes are barred after that point, and Stage One can reject projects that fail basic viability or required-tool fit.
unresolved_claims: Whether entrants currently have a consistent local checklist for all required artifacts is not sourced.
Whether judges will actually test a given project or rely mainly on the demo is unknown because testing is optional.
The exact Devpost submission form fields were not independently accessible without login.

user_class: Small teams building with coding agents in shared repositories
painful_workflow: Demonstrating meaningful human and coding-agent contribution is difficult when work happens across commits, local sessions, README claims, and required hackathon proof fields.
unmet_need: A clearer audit trail that connects new work during the eligible period to the required Codex evidence and explains the role of GPT-5.6 without relying on vague after-the-fact narration.
why_now: Pre-existing projects are allowed only if meaningfully extended during the submission period, and submissions require a repository, README explanation, demo narration, and /feedback Codex Session ID.
unresolved_claims: It is not sourced how often teams are disqualified for unclear prior-work boundaries.
The rules do not specify the exact evidence format needed beyond timestamped logs or dated commit history examples.
No official scoring sheet quantifies how much contribution traceability affects Stage Two scoring.

user_class: Teachers and instructional content creators producing technical learning materials
painful_workflow: Creating accurate, runnable, learner-appropriate coding lessons involves translating complex repository behavior into explanations, examples, visuals, and checks while avoiding shallow tutorial or flashcard patterns.
unmet_need: A way to ground learning material in verified working code and observable execution so learners see what changed, why it works, and where assumptions remain uncertain.
why_now: The Education track rewards working projects with design, implementation, impact, and idea quality, while common generic tutor and flashcard concepts face high collision pressure.
unresolved_claims: The evidence includes a public repository title suggesting code-learning video generation, but does not prove learner demand or adoption.
No sponsor dataset or published gallery is available to validate which education workflows are least crowded.
Per-track judge allocation is not published, so education-specific judging priorities are inferred rather than sourced.

user_class: Operations leads coordinating bounded internal work with AI-assisted engineering
painful_workflow: Moving from a business request to a small working internal tool requires scoping constraints, coordinating implementation, preserving governance, and producing evidence that the result is usable rather than just a dashboard or chatbot.
unmet_need: A disciplined workflow for converting constrained operational needs into testable software changes with auditable state transitions and clear human review points.
why_now: The Work and Productivity track rewards working, coherent product experiences with real impact, while generic workflow chatbots and dashboard-only analytics are identified as high-collision patterns.
unresolved_claims: The public repository excerpt indicates a bounded coding-agent MVP workflow, but does not validate real operational users or outcomes.
Human approval and review loops are identified as potentially underexplored, but no direct user research is supplied.
The degree to which judges prefer irreversible action workflows over advisory workflows is inferred from judging criteria and crowding analysis, not explicitly stated.
